title: Telangana loses 60% of cyber fraud losses to investment scams: Shikha Goel
excerpt: HYDERABAD: Nearly 60% of the financial losses suffered by cybercrime victims in Telangana are linked to stock-trading and business investment frauds, Principal Secretary to the state home department Shikha Goel said at a cybersecurity symposium here on Tuesday. Goel, who also heads the Telangana Cyber Security Bureau and Telangana Forensic Science Laboratories, said cybercriminals were […] HYDERABAD: Nearly 60% of the financial losses suffered by cybercrime victims in Telangana are linked to stock-trading and business investment frauds, Principal Secretary to the state home department Shikha Goel said at a cybersecurity symposium here on Tuesday. Goel, who also heads the Telangana Cyber Security Bureau and Telangana Forensic Science Laboratories, said cybercriminals were increasingly studying human behaviour. They use this knowledge to manipulate victims into transferring their own money. Cyber fraud networks operate across borders Cyber fraud networks have become highly sophisticated, Goel said. Some operate from outside India, including Vietnam, Myanmar and Cambodia. These networks work across multiple layers, locations and time zones. Such operations make it difficult for investigators to identify and reach their masterminds. "They run sophisticated call centres where people from different countries speak in the language of their targets," Goel said. Authorities have recovered ₹455 crore lost to cyber fraudsters over the past two years, she said. "Cybercrime is one of the most organised crimes. At the same time, it is also one of the most preventable crimes. People get trapped because of their fear, greed and ignorance," Goel said. She urged people not to assume they could never become cybercrime victims. "Innocence doesn't work. If you don't want to fall prey to cyber fraud, you have to be intelligent. Trust your intelligence. Pause, think and verify before you act," she said. It was a pleasure to join Symposium’s Panel Discussion on Cyber Security today in Hyderabad on “When Trust Becomes the Weapon - The New Battle for the Human Mind.” We discussed the evolving nature of cyber fraud, including digital-arrest scams, deepfakes, social engineering and… pic.twitter.com/aGntybcZlV — Shikha Goel, IPS (@Shikhagoel_IPS) September 30, 2026 Experts warn against excessive AI dependence Cyber-law expert and Supreme Court advocate Pavan Duggal warned against excessive dependence on Artificial Intelligence (AI). People should retain the ability to think, question information and make independent decisions, he said. "God has given you the ability to discern and join the dots. Use that ability. Don't let that skill die. Don't use AI for recommendations for every small thing. Keep AI at arm's length," Duggal said. Growing dependence on AI for everyday decisions could weaken human judgement, he warned. "People are blindly going gaga over AI. They consider it a life coach, but it can become a suicidal coach," he said. Duggal urged people to exercise caution while using AI-generated information and recommendations. "Outsourcing all our work to Artificial Intelligence will eventually lead to the decay of the human mind," Duggal said. He called for clear legal principles to govern AI and said dedicated laws on AI and deepfakes were needed. Duggal also highlighted the need for accountability for AI-related harms. People should not treat AI-generated information as unquestionable truth, he said. He referred to the draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Courts, 2026, prepared under the aegis of the Supreme Court's AI Committee. The framework seeks responsible AI use while retaining human and judicial oversight. "We have become cognitive slaves to AI. Respect the cognitive minds of people," he said. Cybersecurity experts focus on human trust The symposium, titled "Conversation on Cybersecurity: When Trust Becomes the Weapon: The New Battle for the Human Mind", was organised by Symposium, Hyderabad's knowledge forum, in collaboration with the Telangana State Police, Telangana Cyber Security Bureau and Cyberabad Police. More than 200 people attended the programme at Hotel Avasa in Madhapur. Air Vice Marshal (Dr) Devesh Vatsa, Cyber Security and Critical Technologies Advisor at the Data Security Council of India and a former Indian Air Force officer, moderated the session. Using an analogy from the Ramayana, Vatsa described the Lakshman Rekha as an original firewall — a boundary designed to protect against a threat. "Cybercrime is nothing but greed, lust and fear," he said. Criminals exploit these basic human emotions, Vatsa explained. "We are entering an era where the weaponising of trust is becoming a strategy," Vatsa said. Jiten Jain, CEO of Indian Infosec Consortium, urged people to treat their mobile numbers as sensitive personal information. He asked people not to routinely share their mobile numbers while shopping or billing. Consumers should also question why businesses collect their numbers and how they could use them later. "Your mobile number should be extremely personal," Jain said. He warned that phone numbers could become entry points for social-engineering attempts and identity-related fraud. Cybersecurity enthusiast and ethical hacker Shubhank Singhai said trust could become a more valuable target for cybercriminals than a server, bank account or government database. "We spend billions building stronger encryption, better firewalls and smarter detection systems. Yet some of the biggest attacks today don't begin with malicious code. They begin with a phone call, a message, a familiar face or a voice that sounds just like someone we love," he said. Singhai highlighted the growing threats from social engineering, impersonation, cloned voices and AI-generated content. Speakers said cybersecurity could no longer remain only an information technology issue. It has become closely linked to trust, human behaviour and judgement. Cybersecurity awareness material unveiled The programme also saw the unveiling of public-interest cybersecurity videos and awareness creatives prepared in collaboration with the Telangana Cyber Security Bureau. According to the organisers, the initiative has helped create awareness among nearly 2.95 lakh pensioners and more than 3 lakh serving employees across Telangana. The videos and awareness material provide practical guidance on preventing cybercrime. Gazetted officers associated with Symposium's collaborations will later distribute the material, the organisers said. A paper capturing discussions and insights from the previous edition of the symposium was also presented to Goel. Focus on safer digital decisions Symposium managing trustee Shruti Mallpani said the central challenge was human judgement rather than technology. The forum aims to create conversations that help citizens understand emerging threats and make safer decisions in the digital environment, she said. ]]>

title: Gujarat startup’s thermal infrared camera to launch aboard SpaceX’s 'Falcon 9' rocket on Oct 1
excerpt: Gandhinagar, Sep 30 (IANS) An Ahmedabad-based spacetech startup’s thermal infrared camera, designed to capture heat patterns on Earth that conventional satellite cameras cannot detect, is set to be launched into space aboard SpaceX’s 'Falcon 9' rocket from the United States on October 1. Developed by Satleo, TAPAS-1 is described by the company as India’s first thermal infrared camera developed by a private company. Weighing three kg, the payload will be deployed on a satellite in an orbit about 500 km above Earth and will capture thermal infrared radiation from the surface to generate images showing variations in heat and temperature. The data is expected to have applications in agriculture, urban heat management, water stress monitoring, industrial and disaster monitoring, forest-fire detection and climate-related studies. The thermal data can also be analysed using artificial intelligence to provide more detailed information for different applications. “This data can be used to monitor forest fires. Besides, temperature variations across different areas of a city can be tracked in real time. Different areas of a city have different temperatures. This can help municipal corporations undertake the necessary planning to address heat stress,” Satleo CEO Shravan Singh said. Satleo was founded in Ahmedabad in 2023 by Singh, Dr Ranendu Ghosh and Urmil Bakhai. Singh has more than 16 years of experience in satellite-related innovations, while Ghosh worked with ISRO for 27 years on satellite payload technologies related to agriculture, hydrology and soil science. Bakhai, the company’s Chief Strategy Officer, has more than 22 years of experience in corporate sales and leadership. “This technology will function as a thermometer for the Earth. It can provide highly important data for the agricultural sector. Through this, planning required for crops can be undertaken in a more modern and accurate manner. It can also be useful in urban planning. Most importantly, there is no need to create any large-scale additional infrastructure for this purpose. This data will be available directly from the satellite,” Bakhai said. TAPAS-1 has been developed entirely at Satleo’s laboratory in Gujarat and is expected to remain in orbit for three years. The company said it has a team of more than 40 professionals and plans to launch eight more satellites of the same type by 2029. It has so far secured funding of Rs 60 crore. Following the commercial launch, the company plans to provide thermal imaging data to organisations across sectors. Satleo had earlier undertaken a pilot project with the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation involving temperature mapping across different parts of the city. According to Singh, Satleo has also received Letters of Intent worth around USD 52 million, with about 60 per cent of the commitments coming from companies based outside India. Organisations in agriculture and other sectors are also working with the company. The development comes amid Gujarat’s efforts to build a dedicated spacetech ecosystem. Under its Gujarat Spacetech Policy 2025-30, the state government has announced incentives for startups and private investors, including assistance towards launch costs, support for intellectual property rights and subsidies for testing facilities. The policy is aimed at developing Gujarat as a manufacturing and innovation hub for space technology. The development of TAPAS-1 in the state also marks the entry of a Gujarat startup into specialised satellite hardware and thermal imaging technology. --IANS mys/uk

title: IICT signs MoUs with media & tech firms, Ashish Shelar says 'India to lead the next transformation'
excerpt: Mumbai, Sep 30 (IANS) The Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT) has signed five Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with Motion Picture Association (MPA), India, Centre for Development of Imaging Technology (C-DIT), Kerala, E-Sports Games Federation (ESGF), RioWood and Warm Up Ventures. These MoUs were signed on the second day of FICCI FRAMES 2026, which took place on September 29 and September 30 at the Grand Hyatt, Mumbai. The MoUs that were signed in the presence of Shri Ashish Shelar, Minister of Electronics, Information Technology, AI & Cultural Affairs, Government of Maharashtra, and other senior representatives and stakeholders, are expected to strengthen the engagement between the industry and academia. It will also focus on creating an AVGC-XR ecosystem with the help of exchange of knowledge, industry exposure, and establishing the Kerala State Centre of Excellence for AVGC-XR in Thiruvananthapuram. Talking about the latest collaboration, Ashish Shelar said, “India is uniquely positioned to lead the next transformation in media and entertainment." “The real opportunity lies in building an ecosystem—one that creates professional talent, content creators, broadcasters, developers, technologists, innovators, and entrepreneurs. The future belongs not just to those who consume entertainment, but to those who build the intellectual, creative, and technological ecosystem around it.” he went on to add. Ashish Kulkarni, Founding Director, IICT, stated that these partnerships help to reinforce IICT’s commitment to building a future-ready creative technology ecosystem. Dr. Vishwas Deoskar, Chief Executive Officer, IICT, added, “IICT is focused on building meaningful connections between education, industry and technology. These partnerships will provide our students and emerging creators with greater exposure to international practices, industry-led learning and real-world opportunities.” Urmila Venugopalan, President and Managing Director, Asia Pacific, Motion Picture Association, shared, “We are especially pleased to bring to life a shared ambition that took shape during a fireside chat between MPA Chairman and CEO Charlie Rivkin and Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, which launched the Creative Economy track at the start of the AI Impact Summit in February this year. This collaboration reflects our shared commitment to supporting India’s creative economy and ensuring that emerging talent has meaningful opportunities to engage with the global film, television and streaming industry.” --IANS pm/
